metadata.description:

And BTW, see that string bracelet on my right wrist? The black one? There are streaks of red woven in, even though you can't see them. It's my Archie memorial bracelet.

nodes.plm_caption:
A young woman shows how to cut and tape paper to form a bracelet. In the beginning of the video, the person holds up a pair of scissors and a piece of paper. The paper is placed onto a flat surface, and then a strip of tape is cut. The person creates the bracelet by folding the piece of paper. The bracelet is put onto the person's left wrist.
The woman wears a purple sweater and has brown hair, showing the inner parts of her hands. She also wears a black hairband and has a large ring on her right hand's ring finger.
There are a few objects visible in the background. These include a wall hanging, a white table, a wooden desk, a TV, books and a table lamp.

summary.brief: A young woman shows how to make a pink duct‑tape bracelet.
summary.detailed: The video begins with the woman greeting the viewers and holding up a roll of bright pink packing (duct) tape that she will use for the bracelet. She explains that the sticky side should face outward and measures a length of tape that will wrap around her wrist with a small overlap. Using purple‑handed scissors she cuts the tape to that length, then folds the two ends inward to form short tabs. She folds each tab back so the sticky sides meet in the middle, presses the seam together, and smooths the joint. After adjusting the fit, she slides the loop onto her wrist, notes that a slightly longer size would make it removable, and ends the segment with a smile.

action.detailed: Cut a length of pink duct‑tape, fold the ends inward to create tabs, fold the tabs back so the sticky sides meet in the middle, press the seams together, and then slip the loop onto your wrist.
action.actor: A young woman wearing a purple sweater, brown hair, a black hairband, and a large ring on her right hand.

Holding up her bright pink duct‑tape bracelet, she remarks that she rarely wears it. She then displays a roll of green packing tape, noting that it works like duct tape, and points out a pair of purple‑handled scissors as the only other tool needed. While the bedroom behind her is filled with a desk, books, pictures and a curtain, she measures the tape around her wrist with the sticky side outward, cuts it to length, folds the ends inward, presses the sticky sides together, and secures the bracelet around her wrist, adjusting the size as she goes. She also shows the scissors and points to the blades while describing the materials.

action.detailed: Measure the tape around your wrist with the sticky side out, cut to the proper length, fold the ends inward, press the sticky sides together, and wrap the finished strip around the wrist to create a bracelet.

Okay, you girls on the Indy wanted to know how to make a duct tape bracelet, so here's me on the floor of my bedroom telling you how. :D

And BTW, see that string bracelet on my right wrist? The black one? There are streaks of red woven in, even though you can't see them. It's my Archie memorial bracelet.
summary_sent_to_llm.root_summary: The video begins with the woman greeting the viewers and holding up a roll of bright pink packing (duct) tape that she will use for the bracelet. She explains that the sticky side should face outward and measures a length of tape that will wrap around her wrist with a small overlap. Using purple‑handed scissors she cuts the tape to that length, then folds the two ends inward to form short tabs. She folds each tab back so the sticky sides meet in the middle, presses the seam together, and smooths the joint. After adjusting the fit, she slides the loop onto her wrist, notes that a slightly longer size would make it removable, and ends the segment with a smile.
action_list: cut bracelet and turn off camera
Display watch and pick up scissors
Show how to hold and manipulate the material

llm.system_prompt:
You evaluate YouTube videos for a video-understanding benchmark.

You will be given an Action100M-style summary of one video: title, description,
a hierarchical GPT-written summary of the whole video, and a deduplicated list
of action labels extracted at multiple levels of the video.

Your job is to judge:

1) DOMAINS — does this video clearly belong to either of these target domains?
   - "kitchen": a person preparing food in a kitchen-like setting
     (cooking, baking, food prep — NOT eating reviews, NOT pet-food prep,
     NOT food-product unboxing, NOT restaurant vlogs).
   - "manipulation": a person performing hand-object manipulation tasks
     with clear physical goals: assembly/disassembly, repair, crafting,
     tool use, packing, sorting. The video must show clear procedural
     manipulation, NOT just incidental hand movement (e.g. a vlog where
     someone holds things while talking does NOT count).
   A video can match neither, one, or both. Be strict — when in doubt,
   say "neither".

2) NUM_DISTINCT_EVENTS — count the number of *semantically distinct*
   sub-events (procedural steps) you see in the action list. Merge
   paraphrases of the same step into one. Ignore generic narration steps
   like "speak to camera" or "display title".

3) IS_GOOD_CANDIDATE — true only if BOTH:
   - at least one target domain matches
   - num_distinct_events > 3 (the video shows a real multi-step procedure)

Always return strict JSON in the requested schema.
